title: Positioning narratives and GTM angles by vertical — tradeoffs, hooks, and competitor notes
content:
Executive summary:

This is a working draft of verticalized positioning that emphasizes the operational tradeoffs teams care about (latency, unit-cost, reliability, data isolation). The goal is to give AE/SE teams short, engineer-friendly narratives and one-liners they can use in discovery and early technical conversations. Focus is on the question: 'Why pick Redwood when the options are a cloud-hosted managed endpoint, single-cloud model hosting, or building in-house?'

Key themes (common across verticals):
- Tradeoffs matter more than bells-and-whistles: customers choose based on predictable latency, consistent unit economics, and deployment flexibility.
- Ops-first language wins: talk about SLOs, predictable throughput, and rollback/fallback policies rather than model accuracy claims.
- Deployment model is a primary buying axis: hosted (fast proof-of-value) vs dedicated (predictable capacity) vs private (compliance).
- Demonstrable regressions + rollback path: call out canary rollouts, automatic fallback to cheaper variants, and monitoring tied to prompt sets.

Vertical-specific narratives and value hooks:

1) Fintech / Payments / Trading
- Core buyer personas: infra/platform engineers, head of fraud, ML infra leads, compliance/security.
- Pain points: millisecond-sensitive inference (risk scoring, triggers), cost at high throughput, auditability for decisions, ability to pin model versions for regulated audits.
- Redwood angle: "Predictable inference under load — reduce token cost up to X% via batching + KV caching while keeping 99th pct latency within SLAs."
- Supporting proof points to use: microbenchmarks showing latency at typical sequence lengths for fraud scoring; case example of fallback from large LLM to distilled variant under capacity constraints.
- Competitive notes: Model-hosting clouds (AWS Sagemaker/Azure endpoints) are familiar but often lack continuous batching and cost-aware routing. Other LLM-API providers are simpler but opaque on latency/cost. Red team: emphasize deterministic performance and audit hooks.
- Sales hooks: "Show me the 99th pct latency on your signature prompt for a 200ms target" -> ask for a prompt and benchmark on a demo dedicated node.

2) Healthcare / Life Sciences
- Core buyers: VP Engineering, Head of Clinical AI, Security/Privacy officers.
- Pain points: PHI handling, on-prem/VPC requirements, explainability, model lineage for audits.
- Redwood angle: "Private control plane + optional on-prem runtime with KMS/HSM integration — deploy under your network boundaries with the same API surface as hosted."
- Messaging: stress audit logs, model version pinning, and the private deployment checklist (data residency, KMS). Provide an FAQ on SOC2/HIPAA readiness and what the private package includes.
- Competitive notes: Vertical vendors promise domain models but often require data egress. Emphasize our ability to bring any open model into private, plus quantization options to reduce infra footprint.
- Sales hooks: turnkey POC in a VPC with preconfigured audit log export to Splunk/Datadog.

3) Legal / E-discovery / Contract Review
- Core buyers: Legal Ops, Enterprise KM, Head of Product for contract automation.
- Pain points: deterministic behavior (same prompt => same classification), redaction, retention policies, chain-of-custody for model outputs.
- Redwood angle: "Pin model versions, store prompt-response digests, and tie QA regression alerts to a canonical prompt suite for legal accuracy checks."
- Messaging: highlight reproducibility, canary rollouts for model updates, and integration points for content redaction pipelines.
- Competitive notes: Many LLM-APIs are used as black boxes. Distinguish with explicit reproducibility controls + exportable audit records.

4) Enterprise SaaS (Search, Comms, Analytics)
- Core buyers: Product leads, platform teams, ML engineers.
- Pain points: multi-tenant isolation, unit economics across heavy queries (embeddings search), rollout friction for model experiments.
- Redwood angle: "Scale predictable inference with per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, and built-in A/B rollouts for gradual experiments."
- Messaging: emphasize SDKs, low-friction model swap, and Optimize recommendations (batching, quantization) tailored by route.
- Competitive notes: Cloud providers give infra but not optimization recommendations; APIs give features but not predictable economics.

5) Gov / Defense / Regulated public sector
- Core buyers: procurement leads, security architects, PMO.
- Pain points: air-gapped environments, long procurement cycles, supply-chain/security attestations.
- Redwood angle: "Private + on-prem package with HSM support and a separate control plane option — we map to FedRAMP/CMMC controls in our compliance checklist."
- Messaging: runbook for audits, explicit supply-chain documentation, and recommended hardened runtime configs.
- Competitive notes: Very few providers will do air-gapped on-prem with a private control plane. Make technical onboarding checklist explicit.

Competitor comparison framework (what to bring to meetings):
- Axis: latency predictability, per-token unit economics, deployment flexibility, observability granularity, ops automation (canary/A-B/rollback), compliance readiness.
- Quick table (verbal):
  - Major cloud endpoints: +integration, -predictable token economics, -LLM-specific batching
  - Pure API LLM vendors: +ease-of-use, -deployment options/private installs, -operational transparency
  - Self-hosted open-source stacks: +control, -engineering cost + unknown reliability at scale
  - Redwood: +unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, +cost/perf controls, +rollout and observability focused

Technical FAQs to prep AEs/SEs for quick responses:
- "How do you guarantee 99th pct latency?" -> continuous batching + schedule-aware kernel selection + dedicated capacity SLAs; provide benchmark artifacts.
- "What happens during capacity constraints?" -> automatic fallback to pinned compatible variant or lower-capacity tier with seamless routing.
- "Can we run private with our KMS?" -> yes; outline key integration steps and sample config in the POC pack.

Example one-liners and elevator pitches (engineer-friendly):
- "Redwood gives you cloud speed for experiments and private-grade controls for production — same API, different trust model."
- "Cut per-token billings by optimizing batching and KV-caches without changing your app."
- "Predictable latency at scale: we optimize the runtime for the sequence lengths you actually use, not theoretical maxes."

Sales playbook bullets (what AEs/SEs should do in first 30/60/90 days of an opportunity):
- 0–30 days: discovery focused on SLOs, peak qps, latency targets, and regulatory box-checks. Request representative prompts (and an embedding/response sample).
- 30–60 days: bench POC on hosted vs dedicated: show cost delta and latency tail for the customer's prompt suite. Share proposed rollout plan (canary + fallback).
- 60–90 days: private deployment readiness assessment: KMS, audit log endpoints, approval path, and runbook for failover across regions.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self and follow-ups):
- Create a 1-page POC checklist per vertical (Fintech / Healthcare / Legal / SaaS / Gov) — include sample prompts, compliance checklist, and rooftop benchmarks.
- Gather three anonymized customer benchmarks for latency at 200–800 token lengths to quantify the "predictable" claim.
- Align with Product on a standard set of observability screenshots (per-route cost breakdown, 99th pct latency) for use in AE decks. Owner: Priya.
- Draft a short "technical appendix" that SEs can hand to security teams showing encryption, audit logs, and private control plane architecture. Owner: Marco.

Notes / rough phrasing for decks and email templates (copyable snippets):
- Opening email subject: "Reduce inference cost and make latency predictable — quick POC for [COMPANY]"
- Discovery email body snippet: "We focus on the operational levers you control: batching, KV caching, model variants, and dedicated capacity. If you have a representative prompt or sample throughput numbers, we can show a hosted vs dedicated cost/latency delta in 48 hours."
- Deck slide title options: "Operational economics of inference", "From proof-of-value to production — same API, different trust model", "How we keep your app online when models fail"

References / links to include in final pack:
- Benchmark repo (internal): github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks (link placeholder)
- Compliance checklist template: CONFLUENCE-SEC-215
- Demo kit: JIRA-GTM-1287 (POC playbook)

Rough voice/tone guidance for SEs/AEs:
- Keep it technical and specific in early outreach — these buyers are engineers/security folks. Avoid marketing-speak like "best-in-class" without supporting metrics.
- Use commitable actions: "We will run your prompt on a dedicated node and return 99th pct latency and cost numbers in 48 hours."

Last notes:
- This draft intentionally leans on ops tradeoffs; would like feedback from product and applied-ml on what quantization + kernel selection docs we can safely share publicly as benchmarks.
- Slack threads with questions: #gtm-verticals, #product-hosted-api.

---
Unresolved questions for review meeting:
1) Do we want a canned demo dataset for each vertical (sample prompts + metrics) or allow SEs to request customer prompts for more realistic numbers?
2) What exact compliance attestations can we attach to the public facing playbook (SOC2/HIPAA checklist vs customer-specific artifacts)?
3) Are there legal constraints on sharing microbenchmark outputs for specific open models?

If you're reviewing: add inline comments or drop notes in #gtm-verticals. This should be a living doc — want to keep it concise and engineer-oriented.

(Notes to self: convert final to a one-pager and a short SE cheat sheet with quick rebuttals to competitor claims.)
